column3: Lesson one. You only compare with people close to you.
Look at who Vejeeta picks as a rival. Not the tyrant far above him. Not the fighters far below. The one other Sayan. Same blood, same trade, never far apart in strength.
In nineteen fifty four, the psychologist Leon Festinger proposed that we have a built-in need to know how good we are. And when there's no ruler, we use other people. People close to our own level.
A study of college basketball found the same pattern. Rivalry was strongest between teams that were similar, evenly matched, and had met again and again.
And a review of sixty years of experiments found that, given the choice, we look up, at someone doing better. And it usually leaves us feeling smaller.
Comparing isn't a flaw. It's how your mind takes a measurement.
